titre: The discovery that didn't kill what it's said to have killed
accroche: 1828: Wöhler makes a molecule of life from mineral matter. Textbooks turn it into a legend
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1828, Friedrich Wöhler heats ammonium cyanate, a salt classed among the mineral substances. He obtains white crystals. After analysis, the crystals turn out to be urea, the compound found in the urine of mammals.

He writes to his mentor Berzelius that he can now make urea without needing a kidney, human or canine.

The episode is taught everywhere as the death certificate of vitalism, the doctrine holding that the compounds of living things require a vital force that chemistry could never imitate. It's a good story. It's largely false.

## What the experiment shows, and what it doesn't

The result is real, and it matters. Wöhler obtains a compound previously drawn exclusively from living things, starting from a material that isn't.

But the argument carries less weight than people say. In the processes of the day, ammonium cyanate was itself prepared from materials of animal origin: blood, horn, leather. A committed vitalist could object that the vital force was hiding in the reagent, and some did.

Above all, urea is not a very favorable case. It's a waste product, the end product of nitrogen metabolism, not a building-block molecule. Arguing that an excreted waste relies on a vital force was never the heart of the doctrine.

## The making of a legend

Historians of science have looked at what actually happened after 1828, and the picture looks nothing like the story.

Wöhler himself never claimed to have refuted vitalism: his letter is about chemistry, not metaphysics. Berzelius, who received the news with enthusiasm, remained a vitalist. The doctrine went on being debated for decades, and it was a body of work, Kolbe's syntheses in the 1840s, Berthelot's after that, then the chemistry of metabolism, that slowly emptied it of its subject matter.

The story of the thunderclap of 1828 took shape later, in textbooks, as a founding myth for an organic chemistry in the process of giving itself an identity. A study published in *Nature* in 1944 already called it a legend, and the case has only grown thicker since.

## Why the legend sticks

It has the shape we like to give to discoveries: one experiment, one date, one doctrine collapsing.

Reality is slower and harder to tell. A doctrine doesn't die of a refutation. It withdraws when it stops explaining anything useful and nobody needs it anymore to do their work.

What remains true of 1828 is therefore not what is said about it. Wöhler didn't strike down an idea: he opened a worksite, that of synthesis, which ended up making the idea useless.

repere.texte: A study published in Nature in 1944 already classes the story of vitalism's death in 1828 among chemical legends. Berzelius, the first recipient of the news, remained a vitalist.
repere.source: McKie, “Wöhler's ‘Synthetic’ Urea and the Rejection of Vitalism: A Chemical Legend,” Nature, 153, 1944

carte.punch: Wöhler didn't kill vitalism in 1828. The legend is still going strong.
carte.idee: By heating a mineral salt, Wöhler obtains urea, a compound of living things. Textbooks make it the death certificate of vitalism, but the doctrine survived for decades, and Wöhler never claimed any such thing.

Details, drawing on an 1897 chemical technology handbook, how yellow prussiate of potash was made by fusing potash with horn, leather and dried blood, the source of cyanates and cyanides in Wöhler's day.

quiz.question: Why didn't the 1828 synthesis refute vitalism?
choix: Because the urea obtained differed slightly from the urea produced by the body
Because the doctrine kept being debated, and Wöhler never claimed any such thing
Because the experiment could never be reproduced by other chemists
Because Berzelius refused to publish the result in his journal
quiz.explication: The compound obtained was indeed urea, the experiment was reproduced without difficulty, and Berzelius welcomed it with enthusiasm while remaining a vitalist. It is the reception that undermines the story: the doctrine faded slowly, under the weight of later work, and not because of a single experiment.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where did the ammonium cyanate Wöhler used in 1828 come from, according to the processes of the day?
choix: From an entirely mineral synthesis, with no animal component
From materials of animal origin, such as blood, horn and leather
From the calcination of the bones of domestic animals
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The ammonium cyanate of the period was prepared from materials of animal origin, blood, horn, leather, which allowed vitalists to object that the vital force was hiding in the reagent.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How did Berzelius react to the news of Wöhler's discovery?
choix: He welcomed it with enthusiasm while remaining a vitalist
He refused to believe it and demanded a counter-experiment
He immediately abandoned vitalism and changed fields
He published a scathing refutation in his own journal
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Berzelius, the first recipient of the news and Wöhler's mentor, welcomed the result with enthusiasm without giving up vitalism, which he kept until his death.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the entry, what work helped slowly empty vitalism of its subject matter after 1828?
choix: Wöhler's own repeated experiments alone, in the 1830s
A government decree banning the teaching of vitalism in France
Watson and Crick's discovery of the structure of DNA
Kolbe's syntheses in the 1840s, Berthelot's after that, then the chemistry of metabolism
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text attributes the gradual decline of vitalism to a body of work after 1828, the syntheses of Kolbe and then Berthelot, and the chemistry of metabolism, not to Wöhler's experiment alone.
